First, we isolate the logarithm:

$$
\begin{aligned}{log}_{7}⁡(x+2)+1 & <0 \\ {log}_{7}⁡(x+2) & <-1\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use each side of the inequality as an exponent of $7.$ We get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{7}^{{log}_{7}⁡(x+2)} & <{7}^{-1} \\ x+2 & <\frac{1}{7} \\ x & <-\frac{13}{7}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we must only keep the solutions that are in the domain of the logarithm in the original inequality. To find the domain of the logarithm, we recall that the argument of the logarithm must be positive:

$$
x+2>0\,⇒\,x>-2
$$

Our solution is $x<-\frac{13}{7},$ which can be expressed as $(-\infty ,-\frac{13}{7}).$ Additionally, the domain of the logarithm is $x>-2,$ which can be expressed as $(-2,\infty ).$ To find the solutions that are in the domain of the logarithm, we take the intersection:

$$
(-\infty ,-\frac{13}{7})\cap (-2,\infty )=(-2,-\frac{13}{7})
$$

Therefore, the solution is $x\in (-2,-\frac{13}{7}),$ which can also be written as $-2<x<-\frac{13}{7}.$
